tagline.text: Quiet mist drifting over twin lakes cradled in primary forest

location.label: Location
location.text: Balinsasayao Twin Lakes Natural Park, Sibulan, Negros Oriental

children.text: Lake Balinsasayao and Lake Danao sit in the mountains about
1 hour
by car from Dumaguete. In these quiet volcanic lakes ringed by dense rainforest, you can kayak or ride a raft and enjoy tilapia dishes at a lakeside restaurant — a cool half-day getaway.
Balinsasayao Twin Lakes are two volcanic lakes at an elevation of about
in the mountains of Sibulan, Negros Oriental, roughly

northwest of downtown Dumaguete. Separated by a narrow ridge, the larger and more accessible Lake Balinsasayao sits alongside the slightly deeper, more forest-shrouded Lake Danao, which is why they're called the "twin lakes." Smaller marsh-type lakes such as Kabalinan and Yagumyum are also scattered within the park.

These lakes were formed when rainwater and groundwater collected in a basin created by ancient volcanic activity. The surrounding area is one of the few remaining stretches of lowland and montane rainforest on Negros Island, protected since

as Balinsasayao Twin Lakes Natural Park. "Balinsasayao" is said to come from the local word for the swiftlets that once filled the surrounding forest, and today the area is still home to hornbills, pigeons, butterflies, and other wildlife.

While Dumaguete on the coast can exceed 30°C at midday, temperatures here drop into the low 20s, cool enough to need long sleeves. Mist rises over the lake in the early morning, and clouds often roll down the mountainside in the afternoon to blanket the whole lake. The scenery of deep green forest and mirror-still water offers a completely different feeling from the typical Philippine beach trip.

It's not a place with grand or dramatic sights, but it suits travelers who want to quietly paddle a kayak across a peaceful lake in the forest, those looking to rest for a day between beach itineraries in Dumaguete, and nature lovers who enjoy birds and forests.

You can rent a one- or two-person kayak at the entrance dock and paddle around the lake. On calm mornings with little wind, the forest reflects perfectly on the surface, creating a beautiful rippling scene with every stroke.

If paddling feels like too much, you can ride a bamboo raft steered by a local boatman. Drifting slowly along the lake's edge, it's a great way to listen to the birdsong in the forest, and children and seniors can ride comfortably too.

blocks.title: Looking down on the lake from the viewpoint

children.text: From the roadside near the entrance and the viewing deck along the trail, all of Lake Balinsasayao comes into view at once. Around
, once the mist clears, is the best time for photos.
From Lake Balinsasayao, a forest trail crossing the ridge leads to the even quieter Lake Danao in about
20–40 minutes
. The path can be slippery when wet, so sneakers or trekking sandals are needed.
In the early morning you can hear hornbills, fruit pigeons, and kingfishers calling in the forest. Bringing binoculars adds to the enjoyment, and asking at the park office can get you a local guide.

blocks.title: Tilapia lunch at a lakeside restaurant

children.text: Lakeside restaurants serve simple meals of grilled tilapia, fresh vegetable soup, and rice. Sitting at a hut table jutting out over the water while eating lunch overlooking the lake is one of this place's small pleasures.
Pairing this with Casaroro Falls, in the same mountain area in Valencia, makes for a full half-day nature circuit. Many travelers use a chartered vehicle to cover both places in one go.

Tour the twin lakes first in the morning, have lunch, then head to Valencia for the Casaroro Falls stair trek (round trip about
1–2 hours
), finishing with a sunset view along Dumaguete's Rizal Boulevard toward evening.
It takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
from Manila to Dumaguete (Sibulan Airport, DGT); from Cebu, arriving by boat is more common. Since the airport itself is in Sibulan, you can head straight from the airport to the lakes.
The easiest option is renting a vehicle or van with a driver for half a day or a full day from downtown Dumaguete. The one-way drive takes about
1 hour
; a half-day rental costs about
, or about
if adding Casaroro Falls. Most of the road is paved, but the last stretch has steep grades and narrow curves.
Budget travelers can take a Sibulan-bound jeepney from Dumaguete to Sibulan town or the turnoff toward the lakes (about
20–30 minutes
, about
), then climb the mountain road by habal-habal motorcycle taxi (about
30–40 minutes
). Habal-habal drivers often quote about
one way, or about
round trip including waiting time, so agree on the price and wait time before boarding. You can also charter a habal-habal directly from downtown Dumaguete.
Regular tricycles often refuse the steep sections, so a mountain-capable vehicle or habal-habal is the practical choice.
Twin Lakes is mountainous, so it rains far more often than on the coast. During the dry season from
January
to
May
, the skies are clear and the mountain roads dry, making travel and trekking easy. March–
April
in particular is the best time, letting you enjoy cool air here while the coast swelters.
From
June
to
December

, afternoon rain and fog arrive almost daily, and after heavy rain parts of the mountain road can become slippery or subject to rockfall. Regardless of season, mornings are the most stable weather-wise, and clouds often blanket the lake after
2 PM
. Temperatures run roughly 18–26°C year-round, so a light jacket is needed in the early morning.

Since Twin Lakes is a day-trip destination, most travelers stay in downtown Dumaguete. There are many hotels around Rizal Boulevard and Silliman University at about
per night, and if you prefer somewhere quieter, small resorts and lodge-style stays in Sibulan or at the foot of Valencia's mountains (about
per night) are also available. Simple lodging or a camping area sometimes operates inside the park, but availability changes often, so confirm with the park office in advance.

The signature dish at lakeside restaurants is tilapia raised in the lake, either grilled over charcoal or stewed in a vinegar sauce, along with vegetable-rich soup. Prices are low, but the menu is limited and ingredients can run out in the afternoon. Back in Dumaguete, it's worth finishing the day with seafood from a promenade restaurant or silvanas from Sans Rival.
There are no ATMs inside the park, so bring cash in small bills for the entrance fee, kayak, meals, and habal-habal fare.
Cell signal weakens the higher you go, so agree on a return time with your habal-habal driver beforehand, and if possible, get their phone number.
It's cool and rainy often, so bring a light windbreaker or raincoat and a spare pair of socks.
The back seat of a habal-habal shakes a lot on the steep sections, so ask to wear a helmet and avoid bringing large bags.
Arriving around
gets you both the mist and the reflection shots, and also lets you avoid weekend afternoon crowds.
When kayaking, put your phone in a waterproof pouch, and it's safer to leave a non-waterproof camera on shore.
If you're interested in birdwatching, bring binoculars and a telephoto lens, and walk the forest trail slowly and quietly.
The lake is deep and the water cold, so always wear a life vest when kayaking or rafting. Swimming in the lake outside designated areas is not recommended.
After rain, the forest trail and the dock's wooden deck become very slippery, so wear shoes with good grip instead of sandals.
Collecting plants or animals, littering, and loud music are prohibited inside the natural park. Take out all the trash you bring in.
When heavy rain or a typhoon is forecast, postpone your visit due to the risk of rockfall and washed-out roads.
The entrance fee, activity fees, and operating hours (generally
8 AM–5 PM
) can change according to the natural park's management rules, so check the latest notices.
